tweets: 1/8 A withdrawal function that pays out Ether before zeroing the caller's balance can be re-entered by the recipient, and the second entry still sees the old balance.
2/8 Any external call gives the callee control of execution. It can invoke your contract again before the original call has returned, so your code runs a second time mid-operation.
3/8 Sending Ether is only one trigger. Calling any other contract can open the same door, and state shared across several contracts widens the surface further.
4/8 The flaw underneath is ordering: storage is changed only after control has been handed to code you do not trust, so the same logic can run again and again.
5/8 Checks-effects-interactions fixes the ordering. Verify inputs and permissions first, then write the new storage values, and make external calls last.

6/8 Applied to a withdrawal, copy the amount into a local variable and run `balances[msg.sender] = 0;` before paying the recipient. Also require the payment to succeed, so a failed send reverts everything.
7/8 A callback does not have to come back through the function you patched. It may enter via a different function or a dependency that touches the same state, so audit each of those paths too.
8/8 Does every function that makes an external call finish its storage updates before the call goes out?

topic_name: Denial of service with failed call
tweets: 1/7 An attacker who registers a contract that always reverts as a payee can freeze a function that pays many addresses in one loop, and nobody else in that batch gets paid.
2/7 Ether sends can break for two separate reasons: the recipient runs out of gas, or the recipient's own code reverts through require, assert or revert.
3/7 Solidity's two send styles react differently to that failure. transfer reverts the calling transaction, while send just returns false, so skipping a check on its return value hides the problem.

4/7 A loop that pays everyone ties the contract's forward movement to each recipient behaving. Any payee that can fail on demand gets a lever over the sender's progress, and that is where the denial of service comes from.
5/7 Pull payments remove that lever. Users withdraw their own funds, so a broken recipient only affects itself, and this also lowers the chance of hitting gas limit trouble.

6/7 Give each external call its own transaction that the recipient starts. Keep several calls out of a single transaction, most of all inside loops, and treat every external call as something that may fail.
7/7 Grep your contracts for every loop that sends Ether or makes an external call, then run it in a test against a recipient whose code always reverts and confirm the other payments still work.
